verses.text: Jacob resumed his journey and came to the land of the people of the east.
He looked and saw a well in the field, and near it lay three flocks of sheep, because the sheep were watered from this well. And a large stone covered the mouth of the well.

When all the flocks had been gathered there, the shepherds would roll away the stone from the mouth of the well and water the sheep. Then they would return the stone to its place over the mouth of the well.
"My brothers," Jacob asked the shepherds, "where are you from?" "We are from Haran," they answered.
"Do you know Laban the grandson of Nahor?" Jacob asked. "We know him," they replied.
"Is he well?" Jacob inquired. "Yes," they answered, "and here comes his daughter Rachel with his sheep."
"Look," said Jacob, "it is still broad daylight; it is not yet time to gather the livestock. Water the sheep and take them back to pasture."
But they replied, "We cannot, until all the flocks have been gathered and the stone has been rolled away from the mouth of the well. Then we will water the sheep."
While he was still speaking with them, Rachel arrived with her father's sheep, for she was a shepherdess.
As soon as Jacob saw Rachel, the daughter of his mother's brother Laban, with Laban's sheep, he went up and rolled the stone away from the mouth of the well and watered his uncle's sheep.
Then Jacob kissed Rachel and wept aloud.
He told Rachel that he was Rebekah's son, a relative of her father, and she ran and told her father.
When Laban heard the news about his sister's son Jacob, he ran out to meet him. He embraced him and kissed him and brought him to his home, where Jacob told him all that had happened.
Then Laban declared, "You are indeed my own flesh and blood." After Jacob had stayed with him a month,
Laban said to him, "Just because you are my relative, should you work for nothing? Tell me what your wages should be."
Now Laban had two daughters; the older was named Leah, and the younger was named Rachel.
Leah had weak eyes, but Rachel was shapely and beautiful.
Since Jacob loved Rachel, he answered, "I will serve you seven years for your younger daughter Rachel."
Laban replied, "Better that I give her to you than to another. Stay here with me."
So Jacob served seven years for Rachel, yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her.
Finally Jacob said to Laban, "Grant me my wife, for my time is complete, and I want to sleep with her."
So Laban invited all the men of that place and prepared a feast.
But when evening came, Laban took his daughter Leah and gave her to Jacob, and he slept with her.
And Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to his daughter Leah as her maidservant.
When morning came, there was Leah! "What have you done to me?" Jacob said to Laban. "Wasn't it for Rachel that I served you? Why have you deceived me?"
Laban replied, "It is not our custom here to give the younger daughter in marriage before the older.
Finish this week's celebration, and we will give you the younger one in return for another seven years of work."
And Jacob did just that. He finished the week's celebration, and Laban gave him his daughter Rachel as his wife.
Laban also gave his servant girl Bilhah to his daughter Rachel as her maidservant.
Jacob slept with Rachel as well, and indeed, he loved Rachel more than Leah. So he worked for Laban another seven years.
When the LORD saw that Leah was unloved, He opened her womb; but Rachel was barren.
And Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she named him Reuben, for she said, "The LORD has seen my affliction. Surely my husband will love me now."
Again she conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, "Because the LORD has heard that I am unloved, He has given me this son as well." So she named him Simeon.
Once again Leah conceived and gave birth to a son, and she said, "Now at last my husband will become attached to me, because I have borne him three sons." So he was named Levi.
And once more she conceived and gave birth to a son and said, "This time I will praise the LORD." So she named him Judah. Then Leah stopped having children.

context.author: Genesis names no author. Jewish and Christian tradition, and the New Testament’s way of speaking of “the Law of Moses” (Luke 24:44), credit the five books of the Law to Moses. Many scholars think Genesis was gathered and shaped from older sources over a long time, and a few remarks look back from a later day: “at that time the Canaanites were in the land” (Genesis 12:6).
context.genre: Family narrative: the story of Isaac’s sons, Jacob and Esau (Genesis 25:19 to 36:43)
context.audience: Israel, named for Jacob, learning how God kept His promise through a flawed and struggling family
context.setting: Jacob comes to a well near Haran where shepherds wait with their flocks for the heavy stone to be rolled away (vv.1-8). When Rachel arrives with her father’s sheep, Jacob rolls the stone away alone, waters the flock, “kissed Rachel and wept aloud” (vv.9-11). Laban welcomes him as “my own flesh and blood” (v.14) and asks what his wages should be. Jacob loves Rachel, the younger daughter, and offers to serve seven years for her, “yet it seemed but a few days because of his love for her” (vv.16-20). On the wedding night Laban gives him Leah instead: “When morning came, there was Leah!” (v.25). “Why have you deceived me?” Jacob asks, and Laban answers that the younger is not given before the older (vv.25-26). Jacob takes Rachel a week later in exchange for seven more years (vv.27-30). The LORD sees that Leah is unloved and gives her sons: Reuben, Simeon, Levi and Judah, whose names voice her hope of being loved and, at last, her praise (vv.31-35).
context.custom: Bride-price was normally paid in silver or goods; Jacob, who arrived with nothing, pays in labor. A bride came to her husband veiled, which helps explain how the switch went unnoticed until morning. The wedding feast lasted a week (v.27; Judges 14:12). Each son’s name is a play on words: Reuben sounds like see, a son, and like the verb in her words, the LORD has seen; Simeon sounds like heard; Levi like attached; Judah like praise.
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 30 continues the contest between the sisters and tells how Jacob grows rich at Laban’s expense.
context.timelineBible: The deceiver is deceived: Jacob passed himself off as the older brother, and now the older sister is passed off as the younger. Through unloved Leah come Levi, the priestly tribe, and Judah, the tribe of David and of Jesus (Matthew 1:2-3). The elders of Bethlehem bless Ruth to be “like Rachel and Leah, who together built up the house of Israel” (Ruth 4:11).

translation.meaning: To love. The chapter turns on it: Jacob loves Rachel (vv.18, 30), and Leah longs for her husband to love her (v.32).
To deceive, to betray. Jacob, who took the blessing by deceit, now complains of deceit done to him.
To praise, give thanks. Judah, Yehudah, is named from this verb: “This time I will praise the LORD.”

gospelParallels.note: Jacob the father of Judah, in the line of Jesus.
Whatever a man sows, he will reap in return.
We love because He first loved us.

otBackground.note: Abraham’s servant meets Rebekah at a well.
Like Rachel and Leah, who built up the house of Israel.
Israel served for a wife, and for a wife he tended sheep.

overview.summary: Jacob meets Rachel at a well, serves Laban seven years for her, is tricked into marrying Leah first, and serves seven more; God gives unloved Leah four sons.
overview.settingLine: A well near Haran and Laban’s house.

history.t: A crossroads town of the upper Euphrates, home of Abraham’s relatives.
The sons born here become the tribes of Israel.

customs.t: Jacob pays with fourteen years of work.
The bride came veiled to the wedding tent.

archaeology.t: A mound with ruins from many periods lies at Harran in southeast Turkey.
Tablets from Nuzi and Mari record dowries and maidservants given with brides.

overview.discussion: Leah named her sons after her longing to be loved, until with Judah she simply praised God (v.35). Where am I waiting to be loved before I can give thanks?
overview.book: The book of Genesis · 50 chapters. Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and the nations, then God’s promise to Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph.
overview.author: Moses, by tradition

peoplePlaces.d: Rachel and Leah’s father, out-tricks the trickster
The loved wife and the unloved one

currentImage.caption: Jacob’s Well in the crypt of the church at Balata, Nablus, near ancient Shechem. Genesis 29 is set at a well near Haran, but John 4:6 places Jesus at Jacob’s well in Samaria, and wells run through the stories of Isaac and Jacob.
